title: The talking synth
teaches: Formants, speech engines and Homer Dudley’s vocoder

blocks.text: **The sound.** Here is a plain buzz, then the same buzz singing "ah", then whispering it. Nothing here was recorded. The buzz went through three **formants**, the resonances your mouth makes, set where your mouth puts them for that vowel, and for the whisper, breath noise took the buzz's place. You'll set up the sung "ah" at the end.

blocks.caption: A slow line: a buzz, the buzz singing “ah”, and a whisper

blocks.text: Lesson 2 showed how this works in your own throat. Your vocal folds make a buzz full of harmonics, and the shape of your mouth makes a few resonances, called **formants**, that pick some of them out. The lowest two are enough to tell most vowels apart; the ones above make the voice sound more like a person. A synth only has to copy the buzz and move the resonances.

On a vowel engine, **Wave** moves through the vowels, from "ee" through "eh", "ah" and "aw" to "oo", moving the formants smoothly from one vowel to the next. **Timbre** is the size of the mouth: all the formants together, lower for a big throat and higher for a small one. That is much of the difference between a man's voice, a woman's and a child's. **Shape** is breath: it swaps the buzz for noise, and the voice whispers.

blocks.caption: The vowel engine saying “ee”. Move it through the vowels to “oo”.

blocks.text: Listen to the pitch and the vowel separately. The keys move the buzz, and the vowel stays put. The Wave knob moves the vowel, and the pitch stays put. That's the source and the filter of lesson 2, kept apart.

blocks.caption: The engine singing “ah”. Turn the buzz into breath.

blocks.text: **The mystery.** At the 1939 New York World's Fair, visitors to the Bell Telephone exhibit heard a machine talk. A woman sat at a console of keys, a wrist bar and a foot pedal, and the machine said whatever the audience asked for. It wasn't a recording, and there was no computer. How did she make it speak?

The machine was the **Voder**, designed by Homer Dudley at Bell Labs. It had two sources, a buzz for voiced sounds and a hiss for sounds like "s" and "f". Its filters were a **bank**, a row of ten side by side, each letting through one **band**, a slice of the range of pitches from low to high. Ten keys each opened one band, so the operator shaped the formants by hand, and the foot pedal set the pitch of the buzz. It was the vowel engine, played live. Operators trained for a year, and it was hard work, but in the right hands it was understandable.[^voder]

blocks.caption: The Voder room in the Bell System's building at the 1939 New York World's Fair.

blocks.text: Dudley's bigger idea, the vocoder, was older than the Voder; he had worked on it since the late 1920s. It went the other way. Instead of a person setting the bands, a real voice would set them. A **vocoder** splits a voice into bands and measures how loud each one is from moment to moment. Those levels then open and close the same bands of a different sound, the **carrier**. The carrier can be a synth playing chords; the voice is the **modulator**. What comes out has the synth's pitch and the voice's words.

blocks.caption: A vocoder: a voice's vowel measured in bands, and a saw or noise through the same bands at those levels. Play it.
blocks.task: Hear a vowel with 4 bands and with 16 or more, and try two vowels

blocks.text: The number of bands decides how clearly it talks. Each band is a slice of the pitch range, so the fewer the bands, the wider each slice. With four, each band is so wide that a formant could be anywhere inside it, and every vowel sounds much the same. Around ten bands, words come through, if buzzy. With sixteen or more, the synth speaks clearly. Dudley built the vocoder for the telephone. The levels of a few bands change slowly, so they need far less sending than the voice itself. In the Second World War the same idea, scrambled, carried secret calls between Churchill and Roosevelt.[^sigsaly]

Musicians found the vocoder in the 1970s, and it became the sound of robots and of a good deal of pop and funk. Most hardware vocoders need a microphone for the modulator. A **speech engine** on a small synth is a different machine: it needs no microphone and no voice coming in. It stores a few words or phrases as sequences of formant settings, buzz and hiss, and plays them back at the note's pitch. That's the same thing the Voder operator did by hand, now done by a programme.

The best-known talking machine of all worked the same way: Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell toy of 1978. It stored speech as a stream of filter settings, only about a thousand bits a second.[^lpc] That was compact enough to fit the vocabulary of a spelling game on two small memory chips. On most synths that have one, the three knobs of a speech engine pick the word, stretch or squeeze it in time, and shift the mouth's size, just as the vowel engine's Timbre does.

Now set up the sung "ah" from the opening, starting from the plain buzz. Switch the Engine to the vowel engine, then set Wave to the vowel ("ah" sits at the middle of its travel), Timbre to the mouth's size, and Shape to a little breath. Play the target and yours in turn until they sound alike.

blocks.caption: A plain buzz. Make it sing “ah”.

blocks.text: A touch of breath makes a synth voice sound more like a person, as a real singer's voice is never a pure buzz. The matrix and pressure (lessons 15 and 16) can move the breath as you play.

blocks.caption: Four questions on talking synths
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What makes one vowel sound different from another?
items.why: The same buzz with formants in different places says different vowels.

items.ask: What did the Voder's operator do?
choices: Shaped the formants by hand with keys, and set the pitch with a pedal
Typed the words into a computer
items.why: The Voder was a buzz and a hiss through filters played live.

items.ask: In a vocoder, what does the modulator (the voice) control?
choices: The level of each band of the carrier
items.why: The voice's band levels open and close the synth's bands; the synth keeps its own pitch.

items.ask: Why does a vocoder with four bands barely talk?
choices: Four bands are too coarse to show where the formants are
items.why: With more bands, the formants' places come through and the words become clear.

summary: **A voice is a buzz through formants**; the lowest two are enough to tell most vowels apart.
**A vowel engine copies that**: Wave moves the vowel, Timbre the size of the mouth, Shape the breath.
**Homer Dudley’s Voder (1939)** was played by hand: keys shaped the formants, a pedal set the pitch.
**A vocoder lets a voice set the bands**: the voice’s band levels shape a synth’s sound.
**More bands, clearer words**: with too few, every vowel sounds the same.
**Speech engines store words as formant settings**, as the Speak & Spell did in 1978.

voder.title: The operators
voder.text: Bell trained a group of twenty-four telephone operators to play the Voder, and the training took about a year. Consonants that stop the air for an instant, like "p" and "t", had their own keys, and a wrist bar switched between the buzz and the hiss. The best operators could make it sing, and even say a sentence with a rising question at the end.

sigsaly.title: SIGSALY
sigsaly.text: The wartime system, called SIGSALY, used a vocoder to turn speech into ten band levels and a pitch, scrambled those numbers with a key recorded on matching phonograph records at each end, and rebuilt the voice from them. Each terminal weighed fifty tons and filled a room. The voices it rebuilt sounded buzzy and flat, much like a vocoder in a song, but no one who intercepted the signal could understand them.

lpc.title: Linear predictive coding
lpc.text: The Speak & Spell used a method called linear predictive coding, or LPC. Rather than fixed frequency bands like a channel vocoder, LPC models the throat as a single filter set by ten numbers, enough for about five formants, whose settings shift about forty times a second, driven by a buzz at the voice's pitch or by white noise.
